hints: Focus on the two axes separately, the x-axis order is fixed by a simple periodic trend across Period 3.
Electronegativity increases from left to right across the period, so on the x-axis the order must be Mg, then Al, then Si, then P.
Think about structure and melting point, with giant covalent Si very high and simple molecular P very low, then pick the graph with that y-pattern in the correct x-order.
walkthrough:
**Order the electronegativities**

Think left to right across Period 3. Nuclear charge increases with little extra shielding, so atoms attract bonding electrons more strongly.

$$\text{electronegativity: } \text{Mg} < \text{Al} < \text{Si} < \text{P}$$

**Order the melting points by structure**

Remember bonding type. $\text{Mg}$ and $\text{Al}$ are metallic with moderate to high melting points ($\text{Al}$ a little higher than $\text{Mg}$), $\text{Si}$ is giant covalent with very strong bonds so highest, $\text{P}$ is simple molecular ($\text{P}_4$) with weak van der Waals forces so lowest.

$$\text{melting point: } \text{Si} >> \text{Al} > \text{Mg} >> \text{P}$$

**Combine x-order and y-pattern**

On the plot, left to right must be Mg, Al, Si, P. Vertically, Si must be top, P must be bottom, and Mg and Al must be in the middle close together with Al just above Mg. Only one graph matches both conditions.

options.A: Has the correct left to right x-order Mg, Al, Si, P, but the y-values are wrong. It shows Al with the highest melting point, whereas giant covalent Si must be much higher than metallic Al.
options.B: Correct on both axes. The x-order is Mg < Al < Si < P for electronegativity, and the y-order is Si highest, Al and Mg middle and close with Al slightly higher, and P lowest, matching metallic, giant covalent and molecular structures.
options.C: Shows the correct y-pattern with Si top and P bottom, but the x-axis is backwards. It places P at lowest electronegativity and Mg at highest, which reverses the true increase across Period 3.
options.D: Reverses the electronegativity trend like C, with P on the left and Mg on the right. It also shows Al with a higher melting point than Si, which is impossible since giant covalent Si melts far higher than metallic Al.
